analysis.one_liner: Requires the government to negotiate prescription drug prices for Medicare beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 255-170 on January 12, 2007, with 231 of 233 voting Democrats in favor, but the Senate Finance Committee never acted on it and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2003 Medicare drug benefit, the law specifically barred the Secretary of Health and Human Services from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers. This bill removed that bar and required the Secretary to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates for drugs covered under Medicare Part D, and to report the results to Congress twice a year. It left the private drug plans in place and let them keep seeking additional discounts. The House passed it, but it never received a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of Medicare Part D beneficiaries, who would pay less for prescription drugs if the federal government used its bargaining power to negotiate prices on their behalf. Taxpayers also benefit to the extent the government picks up part of drug costs through low-income subsidies.

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the statutory 'non-interference' provision that prohibited the federal government from negotiating Part D drug prices, and instead requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with pharmaceutical manufacturers for covered Part D drugs.

Keeps the existing structure of private prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans intact, and explicitly allows those plans to keep negotiating even deeper discounts below the government-negotiated price.
Requires semi-annual reports to Congress on the negotiations and the prices and discounts achieved, creating public accountability for the results.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose prices for drugs sold through Medicare Part D would be negotiated down by the government. If negotiated prices reduce manufacturers' revenue, industry groups argued this could mean somewhat less funding available for drug research and development.

drawbacks.text: Opponents argued that competition among private drug plans was already delivering prices below government projections, and that putting the government in charge of price-setting amounts to price controls that could reduce the industry's incentive to develop new drugs. The Barton motion to recommit sought to add protections for continued access to Part D drugs, pharmacy networks, and veterans' drug prices, reflecting concerns that government negotiation could restrict access.

The bill does not create a formulary or directly cap prices; it relies on negotiation authority whose effectiveness depends entirely on the Secretary's willingness and skill in using it, and its six-month reporting requirement is an accountability tool rather than a guarantee of savings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is straightforward: lower drug prices for millions of Medicare beneficiaries, achieved by removing a statutory prohibition on the single largest purchaser of prescription drugs negotiating. The main cost, borne by pharmaceutical manufacturers, is lower revenue on Medicare-covered drugs, with the industry's good-faith argument being that some of that revenue funds research into new medicines. The bill was drawn narrowly — no government formulary, private plans kept in place, plans free to negotiate below the government price — which blunts the harshest version of the price-control objection, but it also means the savings depend on negotiation actually happening. On balance, the upside for beneficiaries is large and the design is moderate rather than aggressive.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House by a comfortable margin in January 2007, but it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never brought it to the full Senate, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 5, 2007 by Rep. John Dingell with 198 cosponsors, and was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees.

On January 12, 2007, a Republican motion to recommit the bill with instructions — adding assurances on continued access to Part D drugs, pharmacy networks, and veterans' drug prices — failed 196-229, with 195 of 202 Republicans voting yes and 229 of 233 Democrats voting no.
The House then passed the bill 255-170, with 231 of 233 Democrats voting yes and only 24 of 202 Republicans joining them.
The Senate received the bill on January 12, 2007 and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where no further action was taken for the remaining two years of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: the statutory ban on government price negotiation remained on the books, and Medicare beneficiaries continued paying prices set through private-plan negotiations rather than government bargaining.

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.role: Sponsor; Chair, House Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 5, 2007 and managed its passage through the House.

for.name: 231 of 233 House Democrats
for.role: House Democratic bloc voting on passage
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, providing nearly all of the 255 votes in favor, and unanimously opposed the motion to recommit.

for.name: 24 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Joined Democrats to vote yes on final passage, providing the margin that carried the bill over 255 votes.

against.name: 170 House Republicans
against.role: House Republican bloc voting against passage
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 170-202, arguing that private competition under Part D was already working and that government negotiation would amount to price controls; earlier in the day, 195 of 202 Republicans supported the Barton motion to recommit the bill with instructions.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction in the Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 12, 2007 and never reported it out, so the full Senate never considered it during the 110th Congress.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed requiring government negotiation of Medicare drug prices and was expected to veto the bill had it reached his desk, giving Senate opponents a reason to let it sit.

sides.party_line_note: In the House, 231 of 233 Democrats voted for the bill while only 24 of 202 Republicans did; on the earlier motion to recommit the split was nearly perfect, with 195 of 202 Republicans for it and 229 of 233 Democrats against.

industries.note: The bill would require the government to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates for Part D drugs, directly reducing the prices manufacturers could charge on Medicare-covered prescriptions. The industry had secured the 2003 statutory ban on such negotiation and benefited from its continuation.

industries.industry: Prescription drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: Government negotiation would cap the prices these private plans pay manufacturers, but the bill keeps the private plans as the delivery channel for Part D and lets them negotiate discounts below the government price, so their role is preserved rather than displaced.
